extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; readers of classical Greek mathematics (Archimedes, Theon, Ptolemy)
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and procedural standards for performing and recording arithmetic (sexagesimal and decimal-like) operations and for choosing rational approximations to square roots as practised by Greek mathematicians (Archimedes, Theon, Ptolemy). Includes notation conventions, algorithms for add/sub/mul/div/square-root, and principles guiding selection of convenient approximations in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal and unit notation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use degrees (μοῖραι) or the symbol αὶ together with the ordinary numeral (with a stroke above it) to express whole units; use one, two, etc. accents affixed to numerals for minutes, seconds, etc.; use the sign O to denote the absence of a unit in a particular denomination (οὐδεμία μοῖρα, οὐδὲν ἑξηκοστόν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ἃ B = 2°; μοιρῶν pl pB’ p” = 47° 42′ 40″; Oa′ β′ O″′ = 0° 1′ 2″ 0. For subdivisions of radius use τμήματα and represent fractions similarly. This prescribes how to record mixed sexagesimal whole-and-fractional quantities unambiguously in Greek notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate-place (vertical rows) representation for multi-denominational numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing numbers for calculation, keep the several powers (units, tens, hundreds, thousands, etc.) in separate vertical rows analogous to modern place-value columns so that corresponding denominations align.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes carrying/borrowing and columnar addition/subtraction mentally and visually analogous to our base-10 practice and was the typical form of Greek sums and subtractions (examples of sums and subtractions are given in the text). It supports performing operations “denomination by denomination.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition and subtraction procedure (denomination-wise carrying/borrowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform addition and subtraction by keeping the separate powers of 10 (or sexagesimal denominations) distinct and carrying or borrowing between adjacent denominations in the same manner as base-10 arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Greeks mentally kept separate columns for hundreds, thousands, etc.; carrying and borrowing operate between adjacent denominational columns (whether the denomination-scale is 10 or 60). Examples show columnar sums and subtractions with the same mental work as modern methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication algorithm (denomination-ordered multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the multiplicand first and the multiplier below it preceded by ἐπί; take the highest power of 10 in the multiplier and multiply it into the terms of the multiplicand beginning with the highest denomination and descending; then repeat for the next lower power of 10, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure applies equally when either or both numbers contain fractions. The text supplies worked examples from Eutocius and Heron illustrating columnar partial-products formed power-by-power and then summed (analogous to modern long multiplication arranged by place value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division (long division) approach by denominational decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform division by mentally keeping terms involving different powers of 10 separate and determining quotient digits by considering how many times a divisor's leading denomination will go into the dividend's highest-denomination block; use multiplication and subtraction iteratively (long division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dividing 608,400 by 780; first determine how many hundreds of the divisor go into the highest denominations, multiply, subtract, and continue. Theon’s sexagesimal long-division example shows repeated subtractions per quotient term in sexagesimal arithmetic; the commentary points out that a method making fewer subtractions per term is more efficient because it reduces unsuccessful trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square-root extraction via (a + x)^2 identity (digit-by-digit method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate the number into compartments corresponding to powers of 10; find the highest-denomination term a of the root, then determine the next digit x by using the identity (a + x)^2 = a^2 + 2ax + x^2 and choosing the largest x with 2ax + x^2 less than or equal to the current remainder; iterate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is exactly analogous to the modern digit-by-digit square-root algorithm. The text gives examples (e.g., sqrt(144), sexagesimal example for sqrt(4500)) and explains trials, remainders, and use of 2a in estimating next digits. The method generalises to sexagesimal fractions by treating fractional sexagesimal places as further denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal-specific square-root extraction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When extracting square roots in the sexagesimal system, express fractional parts as sexagesimal fractions and apply the same stepwise digit-finding using 2a and successive sexagesimal places (x,y,...), guided by geometric intuition where helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ptolemy/Theon examples: find integral part first (e.g., 67 for 4500), then determine successive sexagesimal ‘digits’ x and y by comparing 60·2a·x etc. The text shows mapping between geometric figure and arithmetic identities to locate sexagesimal digits and produce high-precision approximations (example achieving 6-place decimal accuracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting rational approximations for upper/lower bounds in inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing rational approximations used to bound irrational square roots in inequalities (e.g., for proofs as Archimedes does), choose fractional approximations that are either not greater than (for an upper bound) or not less than (for a lower bound) the true value, according to the direction of the required inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary emphasises that Archimedes ensured the chosen fractional part yields a bound of the correct direction (e.g., approximation 'must not be less than the real value' when an upper bound is required). It gives instances where he chooses the fractional part to be slightly too great or too small to preserve inequality direction and correctness of subsequent deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose approximations for computational convenience (divisibility and manageable magnitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer approximations that simplify later computations: choose fractions with numerator 1 and denominators powers of 2 where convenient, or choose values making important subsequent sums/divisions divisible by useful factors (e.g., 13, 40), and avoid intermediate values that produce numbers too large to handle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes often preferred fractions like 1/2^k because they ease arithmetic when added or halved. Examples: selection of fractional parts so that (2911+3014) or other sums become divisible by 13; choosing approximations that avoid unwieldy squares that would complicate later calculations. The text shows explicit choices (e.g., taking 3014 − τ with τ chosen so numerator divisibility works) and explains trade-offs between closeness and convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of acceptable approximation error for proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the introduced approximation error does not affect the final truth of the inequality or the desired conclusion; sometimes a slightly coarser but computationally convenient approximation is used if it can be shown to leave the final bound unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Archimedes sometimes takes a less-close approximation (e.g., 5914 instead of a closer sexagesimal fraction) because subsequent working shows the final result is unaffected; the text explains how he justifies coarser choices by verifying they don't alter the final inequality. This is a methodological standard: acceptable if provably harmless for the intended deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral-part-finding for large square roots via digit-pairing heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the integral part of a large integer's square root, group digits in pairs from the end; the number of such pairs indicates the magnitude (the highest power) of the root's leading digit; proceed by subtracting the square of the highest-place candidate and use the remainder to find later digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Greek notation lacked an explicit zero, the method still applies conceptually by mapping denominations to root-place values (units, tens, hundreds, thousands). Worked example: sqrt(9,082,321) integral part 3013 found by analyzing denominations and dividing remainders by 2·3010 etc. This supports systematic extraction of integral part before fractional refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurrence/side-and-diagonal-number constructions and indeterminate equations to generate successive approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate sequences of rational approximations to surds (e.g., sqrt(2), sqrt(3)) by forming side- and diagonal-number pairs (a_n,d_n) via linear recurrences or by solving Pell-type indeterminate equations (m^2 − 3n^2 = ±1) and using identities to produce further solutions, yielding rationals converging to target surds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theon’s side-and-diagonal-number scheme (a_{n+1} = 2a_n + d_n, d_{n+1} = a_n + 2d_n) produces approximations d_n/a_n → √2. For √3, use identities and recurrence substitutions (Zeuthen/Tannery methods) to produce successive rational bounds; the text explains explicit formulas and sample generated pairs (2,3,5,7,12,17,...). This is a methodological rubric for historically plausible generation of Archimedean approximations.
